name: Dihydroquercetin glucoside
lead: Dihydroquercetin glucoside (DHQG) is described in hair-care marketing as one of the two components of Redensyl, a cosmetic active added to scalp serums and lotions with the aim of supporting hair growth and a fuller-looking head of hair; the other component is EGCG-glucoside. DHQG is a glucoside of dihydroquercetin, also called taxifolin, a flavanonol found in Siberian larch, milk thistle and other plants.[1]

No clinical study of DHQG on its own has been published. It has been tested only as part of finished products: a 2020 randomized, single-blinded, vehicle-controlled study of a lotion combining Redensyl and Sepicontrol A5 in 44 people with androgenetic alopecia reported improvements, and a 2025 study of a rosemary and Redensyl serum in healthy women evaluated hair outcomes for a multi-ingredient product.[2][3] A 2025 review discusses Redensyl among topical hair actives.[4]

paras: Taxifolin is a flavonoid that, according to Wikipedia, has mainly laboratory and animal findings, including reports of chemopreventive and lipid-lowering activity and inhibition of melanogenesis in one study; the article does not mention hair.[1]

DHQG is sold as part of Redensyl in over-the-counter scalp serums and lotions, usually alongside other actives. A 2020 trial of a Redensyl and Sepicontrol A5 lotion used twice daily for 24 weeks randomized 44 patients to active or vehicle; of 26 active-treated patients, 7.7 percent had great improvement, 73.1 percent moderate improvement and 19.2 percent remained stable, with the median anagen-to-telogen ratio rising from 2.25 to 6.02 and no significant adverse events reported.[2] Because the lotion contained more than one active, results cannot be assigned to DHQG itself.

No studies found for DHQG alone. A randomized, single-blinded, vehicle-controlled study of a Redensyl and Sepicontrol A5 lotion in 44 patients with androgenetic alopecia reported improvement over 24 weeks,[2] and a 2025 study of a rosemary and Redensyl serum in healthy women evaluated hair outcomes for a multi-ingredient product.[3] A 2025 review covers Redensyl among topical hair actives.[4]

card.summary: A taxifolin derivative in Redensyl; no studies of it on its own.

quick.overview:
DHQG is a sugar-linked form of taxifolin, a plant flavonoid. In marketing it is one half of the Redensyl hair-growth active.

No study of DHQG alone was found; small studies test finished serums.
quick.mechanism: Taxifolin has laboratory findings in unrelated areas; no hair-growth mechanism is established in the sources reviewed.
quick.risks: Taxifolin is reported as non-mutagenic in bacterial tests; no human safety data for DHQG were found.

chain: Redensyl-type serum applied to the scalp
Marketed to support follicle activity and the growth phase
angle.text: People use serums containing DHQG as part of the Redensyl blend hoping for thicker-looking hair. Trial results are for finished multi-ingredient products rather than DHQG alone.
